about: Ten laws on children taken in and brought up by someone other than their parents. A man who takes a young child (a newborn, perhaps) as his son and raises him cannot be made to give him back (§185); but if, when taken, the child sought (?) his father and mother, he goes back to his father’s house (§186). The sons of two classes of people, a NER.SE.GA and a woman of the zikrum class, cannot be claimed back (§187). A craftsman who takes a foster-son and teaches him his craft keeps him; if he has not taught him, the boy goes back to his father’s house (§188–189). A man who took a child as his son and raised him but did not count him among his sons finds the foster-child go back to his father’s house (§190). If he has set up a household and later has sons of his own and sets his face to cast the adopted son out, the boy shall not go away empty-handed: the father who raised him gives him one third of an heir’s share from his goods, but nothing from field, orchard or house (§191). The sons of a NER.SE.GA or of a zikrum-woman who say to the foster-father and foster-mother “You are not my father, you are not my mother” have their tongue cut off (§192); if they find out their father’s house, turn away from the foster-parents and go to it, their eye is plucked out (§193). The last law is the wet-nurse: if a man gives his son to a wet-nurse and the child dies in her care, and she then takes another child without his father and mother (knowing, probably), they convict her and cut off her breast (§194). The punishments are exactly as the stele states them. A few words (NER.SE.GA, the zikrum class, iḫīaṭ, iṣīrma) cannot be read with certainty; the notes say so each time.

sentences.i: If a man has taken a young child as his son while he was in his waters (that is, a newborn?) and has raised him,
sentences.n: The first of ten laws on adoption and foster-children; like every law of the code it is one “if” sentence, cut here at its verbs. šumma awīlum is “if a man”. ṣeḫram is “a young child” (ṣeḫrum with the accusative -am), the object. ina mêšu is “in his waters”: mû “water”, plural mê, with -šu “his”; I take it as the child’s birth-waters, so “a newborn”, but that is UNCERTAIN — no other use of the phrase turns up in these parts. ana mārūtim is “as sonship, as a son”: mārūtum, the abstract in -ūtum of mārum “son”, in the genitive after ana; this is the adoption formula. ilqēma is “he took, and”: ilqi, the preterite of leqûm, plus -ma (spelled il-qi₂-ma, the KI sign read qi₂). urtabbišu is “he has raised him”: the perfect (the infixed -ta-) of the D-stem of rabûm “to be great”, which means “to bring up”: urabbi (the preterite, “he raised”) has the perfect urtabbi, with -šu “him”. On the plate the first sign of ṣi-iḫ-ra-am (XXXII 32, 40, 66, 76) is Harper’s no. 72 ṣi (a barred box and a hooked upright), not the chevron-stack zi of zi-ik-ru-um (his no. 41); it is keyed ZI, the only ṣi key in the sign glossary, as in the published parts.

sentences.i: No claim shall be made on that foster-child.
sentences.n: The apodosis, and a short one. tarbītum is “what is brought up, the foster-child”, a noun built on the same D-stem as urtabbišu above. It is feminine, so “that” is šī, not šū. ul ibbaqqar is “no claim shall be made”: the N-stem (the passive) present of baqārum “to claim”, as in §112–126 and earlier. Harper prints ib-ba-ag-gar, the AK sign read ag; I write aq, q as everywhere. The law does not name who might claim the child; the next law shows it is the birth-parents.

sentences.i: when he took him, he looked for (?) his father and his mother,
sentences.n: A clause with inūma “when”, whose verb is therefore in the subjunctive: ilqûšu is ilqi + the subjunctive -u (the two vowels contract to û) + -šu “him”, “when he took him”. abašu and ummašu are “his father” and “his mother”, in the accusative (abam, ummam + šu): they are the objects of the last verb. iḫīaṭ (i-ḫi-a-aṭ) I read as a preterite (the shape of ilqi, not of a present, which would be iḫayyaṭ) of ḫiāṭum “to look out for, to seek”: UNCERTAIN, I know the verb only as a 1904-era gloss and the sense “seek out” is what the next lines call for. Nor does the clause say who the subject is; I take it to be the child, who longs for his birth-parents, but the man is also possible grammatically. The verb carries no subjunctive -u, so it may belong to the main run of the protasis rather than to the inūma clause.

sentences.i: If a man has taken a young child as his son and raised him,
sentences.n: A different construction from §185: the young child is introduced first and the rest hangs on him as a relative clause. ša opens it (“whom”), and the verbs of a ša-clause end in the subjunctive -u, here in ilqûšuma “he took him, and” (ilqi + -u + -šu “him” + -ma) and urabbûšu “he raised him” (urabbi + -u + -šu, the BU sign standing for the contracted bû). The “him” inside the clause points back at the child, which English does not need; the English line leaves the relative out.

Plate: the box sign after É at XXXII 80 has the single wedge of Harper’s no. 3 ba (as in a-ba-šu, XXXII 44) and lacks the vertical grid of his no. 4 zu (as in uš-ta-ḫi-zu, XXXII 58); it is drawn as BA, with Harper’s zu and the grammar (bīssu) in brackets, as for his other carver’s slips. UNCERTAIN whether the stele has a slip or Harper’s autograph is imperfect.

another, a second one: ana šanîm “to another”, šanûm “another man” · feminine šanītum “another (woman)”: šanītam, šanītim (ša-ni-tam, ša-ni-tim), in the accusative and genitive · šaniam (ša-ni-a-am, accusative) “another”: šaniam ul uppal “nor shall she pay another (?)”, UNCERTAIN

to bind; with a child, to bind oneself to, to take on (UNCERTAIN in this use): irtakas (ir-ta-ka-aš) “she has bound”, perfect, said of taking on a child; irkusu (ir-ku-šu) “(because) she bound”, preterite with the subjunctive -u, the last sign written ŠU, read as the ending su · verb, G-stem

sentences.i: because she took on another son without his father and mother (knowing),
sentences.n: aššum is “because”, and the verb of its clause is in the subjunctive: irkusu (ir-ku-šu), irkus + -u. Harper prints the last sign as šu, and on the plate it is the horizontal-barred ŠU (Harper’s no. 138), not the gridded su of inakkisū at XXXIII 9 and 40; I read it as the ending of the subjunctive, irkusu (irkus + u), with ŠU standing for su. The rest repeats the charge of the last unit.

morph.gloss: breast (written UBUR, Harper’s list no. 105 tulû; the identification of the character is tentative): tulêša (UBUR-ša) “her breast”, with -ša; the form tulê looks plural (UNCERTAIN), the sense “breast” being singular in the law · noun, Sumerogram

her / its (3rd-person feminine suffix) · on nouns, “her”: after a t the š is assimilated and said ss, spelled with the sign ZA: bīssa (bi-za, or É-za) “her house”, mussa (mu-za) “her husband”, warkassa (wa-ar-ka-za) “her case”, bēlissa (be-li-za) “her mistress”; otherwise written plainly: panīša, mutiša, abiša, šeriqtaša, bēltiša · on an infinitive, the object “her”: ṣabātiša “seizing her” · on a verb-like form: ezibša (e-zi-ib-ša, UNCERTAIN in form) · on a plural noun: mārūša (DUMU{meš}-ša) “her sons”

to cut, cut down: ikkis (preterite) “he cut down” · inakkisū (i-na-ak-ki-su) “they shall cut off”, present plural (the ending -sū is written with the one sign su, as Harper prints it): lišānšu inakkisū “they shall cut off his tongue”, tulêša inakkisū “they shall cut off her breast”

sentences.i: they shall cut off her breast.
sentences.n: The penalty, as the stele states it, unsoftened. tulêša is “her breast”: tulê (the plural form of tulûm, “breasts”, as body-words often are; I give the singular since the Akkadian often means one) + ša “her”. It is written with a single Sumerogram (Harper’s list no. 105, tulû, three connected parts, which I take for the sign UBUR, a tentative identification) and the syllable ša. inakkisū as in §192.

glossary.-ma: and (clause-chaining particle); also “it is X that…” · “only, alone”, on a noun after ša: ša aḫḫīšama (aḫ-ḫi-ša-ma) “that of her brothers alone”; also “and” between verbs: izzazma, iššīma, išṭuršimma
glossary.-ša: her / its (3rd-person feminine suffix) · on nouns, “her”: after a t the š is assimilated and said ss, spelled with the sign ZA: bīssa (bi-za, or É-za) “her house”, mussa (mu-za) “her husband”, warkassa (wa-ar-ka-za) “her case”, bēlissa (be-li-za) “her mistress”; otherwise written plainly: panīša, mutiša, abiša, šeriqtaša, bēltiša · on an infinitive, the object “her”: ṣabātiša “seizing her” · on a verb-like form: ezibša (e-zi-ib-ša, UNCERTAIN in form) · on a plural noun: mārūša (DUMU{meš}-ša) “her sons”
glossary.-ši: her / it (3rd-person feminine singular suffix, on a verb): ukannūšima “they shall convict her”, inaddûši “they shall throw her”, iqallûši “they shall burn her” · iṣṣabassi (iṣ-ṣa-ba-az-zi) “it has seized her” (the t of the perfect + -ši said ss, spelled -zi) · on the present plural: imannûši “they shall count her”, ibaqqarūši “they shall claim against her” · on the Š-stem: ušērribši “he shall bring her in”, ušamṭaši “he has belittled her” · on a verb, the object “him” (UNCERTAIN): inaddûši “they shall throw him” (§155, the man being thrown into the water; the plate shows the sign ši, which elsewhere is “her”) · ilmassi (il-ma-zi) “he has known her”, ilmassima; iḫḫazzi “he shall take her”; išakkanūši “they shall set her (on a stake)” · on a verb of giving, “her”: iddišši (id-di-iš-ši) “he gave her”, inaddinūši “they shall give her”, išarraqūšima “they shall give her, and” · on the Gtn: ittanaššiši (it-ta-na-aš-ši-ši) “he shall keep supporting her”

glossary.-šum: to him, for him (dative suffix -šum, on a verb): ibaššišum “there is to him”, iqbišum “he said to him”, inaddiššum “he shall give him”
glossary.NER.SE.GA: NER.SE.GA (the signs KIŠ, ŠE and GA) — a class of person whose son is named beside the zikrum class and the palace servant (“the son of a NER.SE.GA”); given as the signs only, with no reading and no translation, UNCERTAIN (the middle sign could be another sign than ŠE) · Sumerogram, untranslated
glossary.ablūtum: sonship, the status of a son (Harper’s word, from ablum “son”): ina ablūtim (ab-lu-tim) “from sonship”; nasāḫim ina ablūtim “to cast out of sonship” · ablūssa (ab-lu-za), ablūtiša (ab-lu-ti-ša) “her heirship”, the status or share of an heir (not “sonship” here, the heir being a daughter): ablūssa ša aḫḫīšama “her heirship belongs to her brothers alone”; šalšat ablūtiša “a third of her heirship”
glossary.abum: father: ilik abišu “his father’s fief-duty” · abī (a-bi) construct “father of”: abī mārtim “the father of the daughter” · abim written a-ba in bīt abim (Harper’s spelling, UNCERTAIN)
glossary.alākum: to go: illak “he shall go” · illiku “(where) he went” (preterite, subjunctive -u, after a restored ašar), in the agent law · alākišu (a-la-ki-šu) “his going” (infinitive with -šu): ina alākišu “in his going” · Gt present ittallak (it-ta-al-la-ak) “she shall go away” (the Gt gives the sense of going off; the Gtn would be ittanallak) · ittalak “she has gone” (perfect): ana šīmtim ittalak “she has gone to her fate” · ittalku (it-ta-al-ku) with the subjunctive -u: warka abum ana šīmtim ittalku “after the father has gone to his fate”
glossary.ana: to, for · with an infinitive, “to, for” (ana kirîm zaqāpim “to plant as an orchard”); “as” (ana kirîm), “into” (ana libbi), “at the rate of” (ana itêšu)
glossary.atta: you (the independent pronoun of the second person): atta (at-ta) masculine “you (m.)”, atti (at-ti) feminine “you (f.)”: ul abī atta, ul ummī atti “you are not my father, you are not my mother” · pronoun
glossary.awīlum: man; the free citizen, the code’s first legal class
glossary.aššum: because (of); concerning · because; with a clause, also “so that”, giving purpose or reason (aššum … lā ṣabātiša, UNCERTAIN in grammar)
glossary.aḫāzum-Š: Š-stem of aḫāzum “to take”: to make take, have (a man) take (a wife): ušaḫḫazūšu (u-ša-aḫ-ḫa-zu-šu) “they shall have him take (a wife)” (present plural + -šu “him”) · uštāḫissu (uš-ta-ḫi-zu) “he has taught him”, Š-stem perfect with -šu “him”, the z of the stem and š said ss, spelled with ZU: šipir qātīšu uštāḫissu “he has taught him the work of his hands”; the Š-stem here is “to make learn”
glossary.balum: without · (ina) balum bēl eqlim “without (the consent of) the owner of the field”
glossary.baqārum-N: N-stem of baqārum (Harper BAKARU IV): to be claimed: ibbaqqar (ib-ba-qar, present) “he shall be claimed”, ul ibbaqqar “no claim shall be made” · ul ibbaqqar written ib-ba-aq-qar (with the sign AK read aq) and ib-ba-qar: “no claim shall be made”, said of the foster-child
glossary.bītum: house, estate · bīt karānim “wine-house, tavern” (construct form bīt, written É); bītiša “her house” (É-ša) · bīt awīlim “a man’s house”; bīssa (bi-za, É-za) “her house”, written with É or syllabically with BI + ZA; bītišu (É-šu) “his house”; genitive bītim, accusative bītam, written É alone · bīssu (É-ba(=zu): the plate sign is BA where ZU is meant) “his house”, the t of bītum and -šu said ss: bīssu ipuš “he has set up a house of his own”; bīt abišu “his father’s house” (É a-bi-šu), bīt written É alone
glossary.edûm-D: UNCERTAIN verb, read as the D-stem of edûm “to know”: “to make known, to identify, to point out”: uwaddīma (u-wi-id-di-ma) “he has identified (?), and”, D-stem + -ma; the form and the sense are UNCERTAIN · D-stem verb
glossary.ekallum: palace (É.GAL “great house”) — the crown as owner · ekallim (É.GAL, two signs with no ending written) “of the palace”, genitive after mūzaz
glossary.epēšum: to do, make: epēšim “doing” · to work (land): ippeš(ma) (present): eqlam šipram ippeš “he shall do the work on the field” · to build (?) (a house): bītam ippēšma(?) “he builds a house, and”, the verb broken; iteppuš (?) in a broken line · ippešū (i-ib-bi-šu) “they shall do (work), they shall work” (present plural) · īpušu (i-pu-šu, preterite with the subjunctive -u) “(which) he built”: to make, build (a house) · ipuš (i-pu-uš, the sign BU read pu) “he made”: bīssu ipuš “he made his house”, i.e. set up a house of his own (preterite)
glossary.eqlum: field (written A.ŠÀ): eqelšu “his field” — the fief-land this whole block protects · bound form eqel (eqel itêšu “his neighbour’s field”; eqel ušākilu “the field he grazed”) · eqlam (A.ŠÀ, accusative) “the field”, eqlša (A.ŠÀ-ša) “her field”: eqlša u kirâša “her field and her orchard”
glossary.ina: in, from · at (ina ebūrim “at harvest”); out of (ina bilat kirîm “out of the orchard’s yield”) · “through, by (means of)”: ina maḫāṣim “through beating”, ina pilšim “by a breach”; “regarding”: ina mimma ša … “regarding whatever …”; ina šanat “in the year”
glossary.itti: with · “from”, after leqûm “to take”: itti šarrāqānišu ileqqi “from his thief he shall take” · itti mārīšu “among his sons” (it-ti, written IT, the sign A₂, and TI): the sense “among, in the number of”, after manûm “to count”
glossary.izuzzum: to stand; izzazzu “he stands (in service)” · izzaz, izzazma (i-za-az, i-za-az-ma) “she shall stand (take her place)”, of an heir’s share: zittam kīma aplim ištēn izzazma “she shall take a share like one heir, and”; ul izzaz “she shall have no share”; sense UNCERTAIN · mūzaz (mu-za-az) “one who stands (in service)”, the participle, construct before a genitive: mūzaz ekallim “one who stands in the palace’s service”
glossary.kirûm: orchard, garden (written {giš}SAR, the KIRI₆ sign): kirāšu “his orchard” · kirâm (accusative), kirâša (written {giš}KIRI₆, the -ša written out) “her orchard”: eqlam kirâm “the field, the orchard”
glossary.kânum-D: D-stem of kânum: to convict, prove against someone (uktīn, ukannūšuma) · uktīn (uk-ti-in, perfect, with the infixed -t-) “he has convicted”; ukannūšuma (u-ka-an-nu-šu-ma, present, plural, with -šu “him” and -ma) “they shall convict him, and”; ukānma (u-ka-an-ma, present, singular) “he shall convict, and” · ukannūšima (u-ka-an-nu-ši-ma) “they shall convict her, and”, present plural with -ši “her” and -ma
glossary.leqûm: to take: ileqqi “he shall take” · ilqi “he took” (il-qi₂), ilqû (subjunctive, il-qu₂-u₂), ilqēma (il-qi₂-e-ma) “he took, and”, ilteqēma (perfect, il-te-qi₂-ma) “he has taken, and”; ša … ilqû “which he took” · ilqēma (il-qi₂-ma) “he took, and” (preterite ilqe + -ma, here without a spelled e); ilteqe (il-te-qi₂, perfect) “he has taken”; ileqqi (i-li-qi₂, present) “he shall take”; leqîm (li-qi₂-im, infinitive, genitive): ina kaspim leqîm “in the taking of the silver” · ileqqûma (i-li-qu₂-ma) “they shall take, and” (present plural + -ma); ileqqēma “he shall take, and” · ileqqû (i-li-qu₂-u) “they shall take” (present plural, without -ma) · ilqi (il-qi₂) “he took”; ilqûšu (il-qu₂-u-šu) “(when) he took him”, with the subjunctive -u and -šu “him”; ilqûšuma (il-qu₂-šu-ma) “he took him, and” (with the subjunctive -u before -šu, after ša); ana tarbītim ilqēma (il-qi₂-ma) “he took (him) as a foster-child, and”
glossary.lišānum: tongue (written EME, the sign KA × ME, in Harper’s list the word lišānu): lišānšu (EME-šu) “his tongue”, with -šu · noun, Sumerogram
glossary.lā: not (in subordinate and nominal contexts) · before a noun in the genitive, “without”: lā kanīkim “without a sealed receipt”; in a šumma-clause, “not”: lā ītamar “he did not see”
glossary.lū: or; either (lū … lū “whether … or”); with verb: “let …”
glossary.makkūrum: property, assets — written with the Sumerogram Harper reads ŠA.GA (modern NÍG.GA)
glossary.manûm-count: to count, reckon (the verb; the noun manûm “mina” is another word): imannû(ma) “they shall count” — 3rd plural, impersonal · imtanûšu (im-ta-nu-šu) “he has counted him”, perfect with -šu “him” and a -u- written before it: itti mārīšu lā imtanûšu “he has not counted him among his sons”
glossary.mušēniqtum: wet-nurse, one who gives a child suck (the feminine Š-stem participle of enēqum “to suck”, built from the form; not found in an earlier part): mušēniqtim (mu-še-ni-iq-tim, genitive), mušēniqtum (mu-še-ni-iq-tum, nominative) · noun
glossary.mâtum: to die: imtūt (im-tu-ut, perfect) “he/she has died”, so ina šīmātīša imtūt “she died a natural death”
glossary.mû: water(s); mê nuḫšim “waters of abundance” · ina mêšu (ME-e-šu) “in his waters”, of a child taken while in the waters of birth, i.e. perhaps a newborn, the idiom UNCERTAIN; the form mê is the oblique of a plural-looking noun
glossary.mārum: son (DUMU) — here: a minor, not yet able to sell · member of a group: mārū ugārim (DUMU A.GÀR{meš}) “the sons of the irrigated land”, the district’s farmers · mār awīlim “a man’s son” (DUMU); mārī (DUMU{meš}) “sons” (oblique plural, which may include daughters, so “children”); māršu (DUMU-šu) “his son” · mārūša (DUMU{meš}-ša) “her sons” (nominative plural + suffix); mārīša (DUMU-ša) “her son” (genitive + suffix): ana mārīša “to her son” · mārī (DUMU-i) “my son” (-ī “my”); mārī (DUMU{meš}) “children” in mārī ūlissum “children she bore him”; mārū (DUMU{meš}) “sons” as subject: mārū ana ummātim ul izuzzū “the sons shall not divide by mothers” · mār X (DUMU, the sign TUR) “a member of the class X”, literally “son of X”: mār ummiānim “a craftsman”, mār zinništim “the son of a woman”; māram (DUMU) “a son”, mārašu (DUMU-šu) “his son”, mārī (DUMU{meš}) “sons”, mārīšu “his sons”
glossary.mārūtum: sonship, the status of a son (from mārum “son”), here adoption as a son: ana mārūtim (ma-ru-tim) “as a son”, literally “into sonship”; with the suffix, mārūtišu (ma-ru-ti-šu) “his sonship”: ša ana mārūtišu ilqûšuma “whom he took as his son, and” · noun
glossary.nadānum: to give, pay: inaddin, iddinam, iddinušum; nadānim “to give” · iddin “he gave”; ana kaspim nadānum “to sell”: inaddinūma (present, plural) “they shall sell, and …” · iddin, iddinu “he gave” (preterite; the subjunctive -u in a ša- or inūma clause); iddinma “he gave, and”; …in, …din in broken forms; inaddin “he shall give”: ana damqaršu inaddin “he shall give to his merchant” · ittadinma (it-ta-di-in-ma) “he has given, and” (perfect); inaddinu (i-na-ad-di-nu) “(which) he gives” (present, with the subjunctive -u) · ittandin (it-ta-an-di-in, perfect with an extra -n-) “he has handed over”: ana kiššātim ittandin “he handed over into service”; ittadin (it-ta-din) “he has given”, i.e. sold; ana maṣṣarūtim inaddin “he gives for safekeeping”; iddinūšumma “they gave him, and” · inaddin also of a woman, “she shall give” · inaddišši (i-na-ad-di-iš-ši) “he/she shall give her” (the n of the stem swallowed before -ši), of a sale: ana kaspim inaddišši “she may sell her”, ul inaddišši “she shall not sell her” · anaddin “I shall give”, with the n merged into the k of -kum: anaddikkum (a-na-ad-di-ik-kum) “I shall give (her) to you”; iddinu (id-di-nu) “(which) he gave”; iddinušum “he gave him” · nadānam (na-da-nam, infinitive accusative) “to give”: warkassa … nadānam “(that she may) give her estate” · iddišši (id-di-iš-ši) “he gave her”, preterite + -ši, the n written š: ana mutim iddišši “he gave her to a husband” · inaddinūši (i-na-ad-di-nu-ši) “they shall give her”, inaddinūšimma (i-na-ad-di-nu-šim-ma) “they shall give her, and”, ittadnūšimma (it-ta-ad-nu-ši-im-ma) “they have given her, and” (perfect plural + -šim + -ma) · iddinušim (id-di-nu-ši-im) “he gave her”, with the subjunctive -u in a ša-clause
glossary.nakāsum: to cut, cut down: ikkis (preterite) “he cut down” · inakkisū (i-na-ak-ki-su) “they shall cut off”, present plural (the ending -sū is written with the one sign su, as Harper prints it): lišānšu inakkisū “they shall cut off his tongue”, tulêša inakkisū “they shall cut off her breast”
glossary.nasāḫum: to pull out, uproot; of a son, to cast out, disinherit (Harper: “to cut off, to disinherit”): nasāḫim (na-sa-ḫi-im, infinitive) “to cast out”; anassaḫ (a-na-za-aḫ) “I shall cast out” (first person present); inassaḫ (i-na-za-aḫ) “he shall cast out” (third person present) · inassaḫū (i-na-za-ḫu) “they shall pluck out”, present plural: īnšu inassaḫū “they shall pluck out his eye” (the ZA sign for sa) · nasāḫim (na-sa-ḫi-im) infinitive “to cast out”: ana tarbītim nasāḫim “to cast out the foster-child”
glossary.pānum: front, face: ina pani “in front of” · panīša ištakan “she has set her face”: the idiom for making up one’s mind, resolving to do something; with ana + infinitive “to …” (panīšu, panīša “his, her face”) · idioms: panam šakānum “to set the face” = to make up one’s mind; panīšu wabālum “to carry his face” = to overlook an offence (UNCERTAIN)
glossary.qabûm: to speak, say: iqbû, iqtabi, iqabbûma
glossary.qātum: hand: ina qāt “from the hand of” · qātīšu (qa₂-ti-šu) “of his hands”: bīš qātīšu “his own goods” · qāt (qa₂-at) construct “in the hand of, in the care of”: ina qāt mušēniqtim “in the care (hand) of the wet-nurse” · qātīšu “of his hands” in šipir qātīšu “the work of his hands”
glossary.rabûm-D: D-stem of rabûm: to bring up, raise: urabbāšu “she shall raise him” · urabba (present) “he shall raise (the orchard)” · urabbû (u-ra-ab-bu-u) “they shall bring up” (present plural), with young children as object · urtabbišu (ur-ta-ab-bi-šu) “he has raised him”, perfect + -šu; urabbûšu (u-ra-ab-bu-šu, also u-ra-ab-bu-u-šu) “(whom) he raised”, the preterite urabbi + the subjunctive -u (said û) + -šu “him”; murabbīšu (mu-ra-bi-šu) “the one who raised him”, murabbītišu (mu-ra-bi-ti-šu) “the one (f.) who raised him”, murabbīssu (mu-ra-bi-zu) “his raiser”: participles of the D-stem with the suffix, said of the foster-father and foster-mother
glossary.rakāsum: to bind; with a child, to bind oneself to, to take on (UNCERTAIN in this use): irtakas (ir-ta-ka-aš) “she has bound”, perfect, said of taking on a child; irkusu (ir-ku-šu) “(because) she bound”, preterite with the subjunctive -u, the last sign written ŠU, read as the ending su · verb, G-stem
glossary.rašûm: to get, acquire: irtaši “he has acquired”, iraššû “he acquires” · iršû (ir-šu-u) “(whom) he has acquired” (the relative -u): ana mārī ša iršû “for the sons whom he has acquired”
glossary.rēqum: empty (the adjective): rīqūssu (ri-qu₂-zu) “empty-handed (?)”, a reading from the signs RI + QU + ZU, probably rīqūtum “emptiness” + -šu (t + š said ss, spelled with ZU), used as an adverb; Harper prints tal-ku-zu; the form and the sense “empty-handed” are both UNCERTAIN · adjective / adverb (uncertain)
glossary.tarbītum: a foster-child, one who is brought up (from the D-stem of rabûm “to bring up”, tarbītum “what is raised”): tarbītum (tar-bi-tum, nominative), tarbītim (tar-bi-tim, genitive after ana): ana tarbītim ilqēma “he took (him) as a foster-child, and”; the same child as mārūtum seen from the side of the one raised · noun
glossary.tulûm: breast (written UBUR, Harper’s list no. 105 tulû; the identification of the character is tentative): tulêša (UBUR-ša) “her breast”, with -ša; the form tulê looks plural (UNCERTAIN), the sense “breast” being singular in the law · noun, Sumerogram
glossary.târum: to return: ul itârma “he shall never again …” · itâr (i-ta-ar) “he shall go back”: ana bīt abišu itâr “he shall go back to his father’s house”
glossary.ummiānum: a craftsman, a skilled worker (written with the Sumerograms UM.MI.A, three signs UM, MI, A, with no ending written): ummiānim “of a craftsman” (genitive, read from the context); mār ummiānim “a craftsman”, literally “a son of a craftsman” (see mārum) · noun, Sumerogram
glossary.ummum: mother: ana ummišu “to his mother”, ummašu urabbāšu “his mother shall raise him” · ummātim (um-ma-tim) plural “mothers”: ana ummātim “by mothers”; ummātišunu “their mothers”
glossary.warka: afterwards, later · as a conjunction before a clause, “after”: warka abum ana šīmtim ittalku “after the father has gone to his fate”
glossary.zikrum-class: zikrum (zi-ik-ru-um) — the name of a class of woman, named beside the ugbabtum (NIN.AN) in §178–179 and beside the kallātim in §180; it is not zikrum “name” of the prologue, and what the class was is not known, UNCERTAIN · noun · zikrum also in mār zinništim zikrum “the son of a woman, a zikrum”, still UNCERTAIN
glossary.zinništum: woman (written with the single sign SAL, ŠAL in Harper): zinništam, zinništim, zinništum
glossary.īnum: eye: īnšu … iššīma “he lifted his eye (to it)” — he coveted it · ša īnšu maḫru (i-in-šu) “whose eye is first” = the son he favours (UNCERTAIN idiom)
glossary.šakānum: to set, place: išakkanūšumma “they shall set for him (a term), and” · išakkanūšum (present, plural, dative -šum) “they shall place (it) for him”, i.e. count it to him · iššakkan (iš-ša-ak-ka-an, N-stem present) “it shall be put”: ul iššakkan “it shall not be put (in the account)” · to set, put, impose: ištakan (iš-ta-ka-an, perfect, “has set”), išakkan (present) — išakkanšima (i-ša-ak-ka-an-ši-ma, with -ši and -ma) “he/she shall set (it) on her, and”, as in abbuttam išakkan · išakkanūši “they shall set (her on a stake)”, išakkanūšumma “they shall set (it) aside for him, and” · idiom panam šakānum (panam ištakan) “to set the face” = to make up one’s mind · iššakkan also written iš-ta-ak-ka-an (Harper’s reading, UNCERTAIN): andurār amtim iššakkan “the release of the slave-woman shall be established”
glossary.šalšum: a third, one third (written IGI.3.GAL, three signs: IGI, the numeral 3, GAL): before a following noun šalšat “one third of”, a reconstructed construct form, marked (?) in the gloss: šalšat ablūtiša “a third of her heirship” · numeral / fraction, Sumerogram
glossary.šanûm: another, a second one: ana šanîm “to another”, šanûm “another man” · feminine šanītum “another (woman)”: šanītam, šanītim (ša-ni-tam, ša-ni-tim), in the accusative and genitive · šaniam (ša-ni-a-am, accusative) “another”: šaniam ul uppal “nor shall she pay another (?)”, UNCERTAIN
glossary.šiprum: work, labour: šiprim “of work” · šipir (ši-pi₂-ir) construct “the work of”: šipir qātīšu “the work of his hands”, the craft taught to a son
glossary.šumma: if — the word that opens every law of the code
glossary.šī: she, that (feminine pronoun, as the independent word): ŠAL.GEŠ.TIN.NA šī “that tavern-keeper”; the masculine is šū
glossary.ḫiāṭum: UNCERTAIN verb, the root not settled; read from the context as “to look out for, to seek out”: iḫīaṭ (i-ḫi-a-aṭ) “he looked for (?)”, said of seeking a father and mother; who the subject is, the man or the child, is also UNCERTAIN · verb
glossary.ṣeḫrum: young; the child: mār awīlim ṣeḫram “the young son of a free man” · plural ṣiḫḫirū (ṣi-iḫ-ḫi-ru) “(who are) small”, said of children, and ṣiḫḫirūtim (ṣi-iḫ-ḫi-ru-tim) “the small ones”; UNCERTAIN whether the first is a stative or the plural of the adjective
glossary.ṣiārum: UNCERTAIN verb, the root not settled (perhaps a hollow verb ṣiārum); read from the context as “to turn away from, to leave”: iṣīrma (i-ṣi-ir-ma) “he has turned away from (?), and”, with -ma; the sense follows the sequence of the law · verb
